title: Stellantis would owe feds $831M if sale of Brampton, Ont., plant proceeds: source
byline: Darren Major, Janyce McGregor, Peter Zimonjic

image.caption: Unifor members picket outside the Stellantis-owned Chrysler Brampton assembly plant last week. The shuttered plant is slated to be sold to an armoured vehicle-maker Roshel. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

blocks.text: Politics
The projected amount of money Stellantis would owe Ottawa should the sale of its Brampton, Ont., auto plant proceed is $831 million, a senior federal source tells CBC News.
Stellantis losing money over emissions standards and tariffs, Premier Ford says
· CBC News
· Posted: Nov 20, 2026 2:09 PM EST | Last Updated: 4 hours ago
The projected amount of money Stellantis would owe Ottawa should the sale of its Brampton, Ont., auto plant proceed is about $831 million, a senior federal source tells CBC News.
The source confirmed the number after Ontario Premier Doug Ford said the automaker owes the federal government "roughly" $873 million.

The company met with Ford, federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and union representatives in Toronto on Friday afternoon after it confirmed the planned sale of the plant to armoured ⁠vehicle-maker Roshel Inc. last week.
Ottawa has threatened to sue Stellantis for the federal support it was given as part of a 2022 agreement if that sale goes ahead.
Joly hasn't explicitly said how much money the federal government has given Stellantis since that agreement was struck, only suggesting it was "hundreds of millions."
The company said it would pay back $24 million after it announced the sale.
Ford says Stellantis owes Ottawa 'roughly' $873M
Speaking to reporters following Friday's meeting, Ford said the company made it clear that U.S. tariffs and greenhouse gas emission standards were making the factory unviable.
"We got a big problem here and the federal government needs to listen," Ford said.
The premier said the meeting was "challenging" but "productive."

Last month, the federal government moved to hold emissions standards flat until 2030 — maintaining 2026 levels for new light-duty vehicles through the 2029 model year. That move came after the Trump administration made similar changes.
Lana Payne — the national president of Unifor, the union representing workers at the plant — said the emissions standards have been an "irritant" for the industry since the U.S. changed its policies.

"This is one of the things that is in our control, to take away what is a major problem for the auto industry in this moment — and I suggest we get down to doing that," she told reporters following Friday's meeting.
"The tariff situation, that's another problem. But while we're facing that we need to take away any own goals."

items: Feds say Stellantis owes 'hundreds of millions'

blocks.text: Payne said the governments and the company agreed to keep discussions going into next week.
Neither Joly nor a Stellantis representative spoke to reporters following Friday's meeting.
The company put out a statement saying "we remain committed to continuing constructive discussions."
In 2022, the Trudeau government promised to inject up to $529 million in Stellantis plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., to help them increase production of electric and gas-powered vehicles.
More than 2,000 workers at the Brampton plant have been out of work since the company halted operations in 2023 to begin retooling so the facility could produce the Jeep Compass.
Stellantis paused that effort in early 2025, and said in October of that year that the Jeep Compass would be built at the Belvidere Assembly Plant in Illinois instead.
An 'aggressive package'

Joly said last week that the federal and Ontario governments were preparing an "aggressive package" they wanted to present to Stellantis global CEO Antonio Filosa in the hopes that he could be convinced to stop the sale.

The minister said that if Stellantis is willing to stay and build cars in Brampton, both governments are prepared invest in the company going forward. But if it decides to leave, the federal government says it will sue.

"They need to protect the workers. If not, we'll get our money back," Joly said. "Our goal is clear. If they go ahead and sell the plant, well then they will face legal recourses from the government."
Ford, Joly to meet with Stellantis CEO regarding Brampton plant sale

Last December, CBC News confirmed that the federal government had given $222 million to the Canadian arm of Stellantis between 2023 and 2025. Joly told CBC's Rosemary Barton Live last week that the actual total is "more than that," without specifying how much.
Joly said again on Friday that contracts signed when the federal government invested in the company linked investments at the Brampton facility with investments in Windsor.
"The contracts are clear," Joly said. "We're confident in our position that they're exposed for hundreds of millions of dollars."
